interactions.summary: Jiang returns to Purgatorio, using the terrace of pride to ask why purgatorial suffering differs from hell and pushing students toward the idea that hope and willing participation change the meaning of punishment.

claims.claim: Jiang interprets the burdened penitents on the terrace of pride as people learning humility through a weight that counteracts their former self-exaltation.
A student answer Jiang ratifies is that purgatorial suffering differs from hell because the penitents want the discipline and understand its purpose.
Jiang accepts hope as another decisive differentiator: those in purgatory endure punishment with the expectation of paradise rather than in closed despair.
Jiang keeps the pressure on by saying the phenomenology still looks similar, so the real explanation must go deeper than external pain alone.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns the terrace reading into a diagnostic question: why is the same burden redemption here but damnation elsewhere?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It opens the lecture's major anthropological claim that attitude and will change the nature of suffering.

signature_moments.moment: Hope is named as the force that lets the same physical ordeal become self-punishment ordered toward heaven rather than mere torment.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens the moral and temporal orientation that separates purgatory from hell.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture pivots from aesthetics back to Dante's moral cosmology, making the distinction between hell and purgatory the next central problem.
